section.title: The Greatest Commandment
section.sectionRationale: This chapter holds the Shema, the confession and command that Jesus names as the greatest commandment in the whole law, making it the theological center not only of Deuteronomy's statutes but of Israel's entire relationship with God.
section.thesis: At the heart of Moses' address stands the Shema: the LORD is one, and Israel must love Him with all their heart, soul, and strength, teaching these words continually to their children so that prosperity in the land never displaces wholehearted devotion to Him.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the purpose of the commandments; the Shema itself, hear, love, and teach; the warning against forgetting God in prosperity; the warning against testing the LORD; and teaching the next generation why these statutes matter.

units.label: The purpose of the commandments
units.note: so that you may fear the LORD

verses.text: These are the commandments and statutes and ordinances that the LORD your God has instructed me to teach you to follow in the land that you are about to enter and possess,

so that you and your children and grandchildren may fear the LORD your God all the days of your lives by keeping all His statutes and commandments that I give you, and so that your days may be prolonged.
Hear, O Israel, and be careful to observe them, so that you may prosper and multiply greatly in a land flowing with milk and honey, just as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has promised you.

units.label: The Shema: hear, love, and teach
units.note: with all your heart, soul, and strength

verses.text: {{shema|Hear}}, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is {{echad|One}}.
And you shall {{ahav|love}} the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength.
These words I am commanding you today are to be upon your hearts.
And you shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up.
Tie them as reminders on your hands and bind them on your foreheads.
Write them on the doorposts of your houses and on your gates.
And when the LORD your God brings you into the land He swore to your fathers, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, that He would give you, a land with great and splendid cities that you did not build,
with houses full of every good thing with which you did not fill them, with wells that you did not dig, and with vineyards and olive groves that you did not plant, and when you eat and are satisfied,
be careful not to forget the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
Fear the LORD your God, serve Him only, and take your oaths in His name.
Do not follow other gods, the gods of the peoples around you.
For the LORD your God, who is among you, is a jealous God. Otherwise the anger of the LORD your God will be kindled against you, and He will wipe you off the face of the earth.
Do not {{nasah|test}} the LORD your God as you tested Him at Massah.
You are to diligently keep the commandments of the LORD your God and the testimonies and statutes He has given you.
Do what is right and good in the sight of the LORD, so that it may be well with you and that you may enter and possess the good land that the LORD your God swore to give your fathers,
driving out all your enemies before you, as the LORD has said.
In the future, when your son asks, “What is the meaning of the decrees and statutes and ordinances that the LORD our God has commanded you?”
then you are to tell him, “We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt, but the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand.
Before our eyes the LORD inflicted great and devastating signs and wonders on Egypt, on Pharaoh, and on all his household.
But He brought us out from there to lead us in and give us the land that He had sworn to our fathers.
And the LORD commanded us to observe all these statutes and to fear the LORD our God, that we may always be prosperous and preserved, as we are to this day.
And if we are careful to observe every one of these commandments before the LORD our God, as He has commanded us, then that will be our righteousness.”

shema.gloss: Hear, listen, and by implication obey. In Hebrew thought, truly hearing always includes responding in action; this single word gives its name to the whole confession that follows, and to the daily prayer built from this passage.

echad.gloss: One, unique, undivided. Declares the LORD's exclusive uniqueness against every rival god, and can also carry a sense of composite unity, as in 'one flesh' (Genesis 2:24), language the New Testament later develops in describing the one God known as Father, Son, and Spirit.

ahav.gloss: To love. In covenant contexts this is not primarily an emotion but a loyal, active devotion, the same word used of covenant love between a suzerain and vassal, demanding whole-person allegiance expressed in obedience.

nasah.gloss: To test, to try, to put to the proof. Used of Israel demanding proof of God's presence at Massah rather than trusting what He had already shown them; the word describes presumption rather than legitimate faith seeking understanding.

basic.context: This chapter contains the Shema, Israel's foundational confession that the LORD alone is God, and the command to love Him with everything, heart, soul, and strength, teaching it continually to the next generation as they enter a land of abundance that could easily make them forget Him.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage is both confession and command for Israel's specific covenant life, and Jesus Himself lifts its core straight into the New Testament as the greatest commandment of all, showing its truth was never merely bound to old-covenant Israel but expresses God's unchanging claim on every person's whole heart.
basic.originalLanguages: Shema, hear, implies hearing that results in obedience, not passive listening. Echad, one, declares the LORD's exclusive uniqueness, and the New Testament later finds in this same language room for the one God to be known as Father, Son, and Spirit. Ahav, love, describes loyal, active devotion, not mere feeling, and Israel is warned against nasah, testing God presumptuously rather than trusting Him.
basic.typology: Israel's call to teach these words continually to their children anticipates the New Testament's call for households to raise children in the instruction of the Lord, Ephesians 6:4, while the whole-hearted love commanded here finds its only perfect fulfillment in Christ, the one person who has ever loved God with total, undivided devotion.
basic.christ: When asked for the greatest commandment, Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 6:4-5 directly, Mark 12:29-30, naming it first and foundational, with love of neighbor as its necessary companion. Christ alone fulfills this command perfectly on behalf of His people, and by His Spirit He begins to write this same love into believers' hearts.
basic.god: God is one, utterly unique, tolerating no rival, yet He is also intensely relational, desiring not mere external compliance but total, wholehearted love; He warns against forgetting Him in prosperity precisely because He knows comfort more easily displaces devotion than hardship does.
basic.crossReferences: Mark 12:29-30 records Jesus naming this passage the greatest commandment. Matthew 4:7 shows Jesus refusing to test God, quoting Deuteronomy 6:16 against the devil. Ephesians 6:4 echoes the call to teach children diligently. Romans 10:5-13 reflects on righteousness through faith rather than mere legal observance.
basic.oneStory: This is the theological heartbeat of the whole Old Testament: one God, deserving total love, to be taught continually to every generation. Jesus confirms it as the greatest commandment and, by living it perfectly and giving His Spirit, makes it possible for His people to actually begin to love God as this chapter commands.

context.literary:
Chapter 6 is where Moses begins to preach the first of the ten words. Chapter 5 closed with God telling Moses to stand with Him and receive 'all the commandments and statutes and ordinances,' Deuteronomy 5:31, and 6:1 opens with exactly that phrase. What follows is the first instalment of that teaching, and it goes straight to the root: whom Israel loves.

The chapter moves in a clear line. Verses 1 to 3 state the purpose of the commands, fear of the LORD across three generations and life in the land, and end with 'Hear, O Israel,' which leads directly into the Shema. Verses 4 to 9 are the centre: a confession, a command to love, and a set of practices that carry the words into every place and hour. Verses 10 to 19 look ahead to life in the land with two warnings, do not forget, verse 12, and do not test, verse 16. Verses 20 to 25 close with a child's question and a father's answer.

Two patterns stand out. First, the chapter is framed by generations. It begins with 'you and your children and grandchildren,' verse 2, and ends with a son asking what the laws mean, verse 20. The Shema is placed between them as the thing each generation must hand to the next. Second, the teaching in verse 7 uses paired opposites, sitting and walking, lying down and getting up, a way of saying 'all the time and everywhere.' Hands and foreheads, doorposts and gates in verses 8 and 9 do the same for the body and the home. Moses is describing a life so saturated with these words that nothing is left outside them.

The chapter also turns love into a command. Deuteronomy 4:37 spoke of God's love for the fathers and Deuteronomy 5:10 of 'those who love Me'; here Israel is told to love Him, and it will return again at Deuteronomy 10:12, 11:1 and 30:6.
context.historical:
The first hearers stood on the edge of Canaan, a land of walled towns, cisterns, terraced vineyards and olive groves that had been worked for centuries. Verses 10 and 11 list what they would inherit without labour: cities, houses 'full of every good thing,' wells, vineyards and olive groves. Joshua 24:13 later confirms it happened, 'cities that you did not build ... vineyards and olive groves that you did not plant.' Nehemiah 9:25-26 records what followed: 'they ate and were filled; they grew fat,' and then rebelled.

The warning in verse 16 names a place the older hearers remembered. At Rephidim the people quarrelled for water and tested the LORD, asking, 'Is the LORD among us or not?' Exodus 17:7. Moses answers that question in advance in verse 15: 'the LORD your God, who is among you, is a jealous God.' His presence among them is not in doubt; the danger is how they treat it.

The practices of verses 8 and 9 became part of Jewish life. By the time of Jesus many Jews wore small leather boxes containing scripture passages, called phylacteries or tefillin, on the arm and forehead, and fixed a small case with these words, a mezuzah, to the doorpost. Examples of both have been found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Jesus criticised those who 'broaden their phylacteries' for show, Matthew 23:5, but not the practice itself. The phrase 'when you lie down and when you get up' was taken to mean evening and morning, and reciting the Shema at those times became the heart of Jewish daily prayer, which the Mishnah takes up in its very first question. A papyrus from Egypt dating to around the second or first century BC, the Nash Papyrus, sets the ten commandments and the Shema side by side, a sign of how these texts were already read together.

In the ancient world households were the first school. There were no public classrooms for most children; faith and memory passed from parents to children at home, which is the setting verse 7 assumes.
context.canonical:
The Shema echoes through the rest of Scripture. Deuteronomy 11:18-20 repeats its practices almost word for word, and Deuteronomy 10:12 restates its demand: 'to love Him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul.' Deuteronomy 30:6 promises that God Himself will circumcise Israel's hearts 'and you will love Him with all your heart and with all your soul,' turning the command into a gift. Josiah is remembered in exactly these terms: he 'turned to the LORD with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his strength,' 2 Kings 23:25, after the book of the law was rediscovered.

The prophets carry the confession forward. Isaiah 44:6 and 45:22 insist there is no God but the LORD, and Zechariah 14:9 looks to the day when 'the LORD alone, and His name alone' will be King over all the earth. Psalm 78:4-7 takes up verse 7, one generation telling the next so that they would not forget His works.

In the New Testament Jesus names Deuteronomy 6:4-5 the first and greatest commandment, Mark 12:29-30 and Matthew 22:37-38, and a scribe agrees that God is one and that loving Him is more than all sacrifices, Mark 12:32-33. A lawyer quotes it in Luke 10:27, leading to the parable of the good Samaritan. Jesus answers the devil three times from Deuteronomy, twice from this chapter: 'Do not put the Lord your God to the test,' Matthew 4:7, from verse 16, and 'Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only,' Matthew 4:10, from verse 13. Paul restates the Shema in 1 Corinthians 8:6 and Romans 3:30, and James 2:19 warns that merely believing God is one is not enough.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses meant Israel to understand that the whole law flows from a single relationship. The commandments, statutes and ordinances of verse 1 are not a list of separate rules but the shape of love for one God. Before he gives a single statute in chapters 12 to 26, he tells them what the statutes are for.

He also meant them to see the particular danger of the land. The wilderness had taught dependence by hunger; Canaan would test them by abundance. Verses 10 to 12 are carefully worded: everything listed is something 'you did not build,' 'did not fill,' 'did not dig,' 'did not plant.' The goods are gifts, and the temptation is to enjoy the gifts while forgetting the Giver. Moses wanted Israel to know that satisfaction, verse 11, is more dangerous than thirst.

Finally, he meant faith to be passed on in the ordinary life of the home, and he wanted parents ready with an answer. When a child asks what the laws mean, verse 20, the answer is not a list of rules but a story: we were slaves, the LORD brought us out, He brought us in, and He commanded these things for our good, verses 21 to 24. Moses wanted every Israelite household to understand that law is explained by grace.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The call to love the one God with the whole self is not limited to Israel's national covenant. Jesus names it the first and greatest commandment for everyone, Mark 12:29-30, and the New Testament treats it as the heart of the Christian life, 1 Corinthians 8:6 and 1 Corinthians 16:22.

Some elements are tied to Israel's situation. The promise of long life and prosperity in 'the good land,' verses 3 and 18, belongs to Israel's covenant in Canaan and should not be turned into a promise of material success. The threat in verse 15 addresses Israel as a nation in the land. The practices of verses 8 and 9 may be followed literally, as many Jews do, or taken as vivid commands to saturate body and home with God's word; the text itself is concerned with the words being 'upon your hearts,' verse 6.

What carries forward directly is the pattern. Christian parents are called to raise their children 'in the discipline and instruction of the Lord,' Ephesians 6:4, in ordinary moments at home and on the road, and to explain God's commands by telling the story of redemption.

debates.question: What exactly does verse 4 assert?

views.label: The LORD is uniquely one
views.case: The verse affirms that the LORD is the only true God, in line with Deuteronomy 4:35 and 4:39, 'there is no other.' The oneness is both uniqueness, He belongs to no class of gods, and integrity, He is not divided into many local or partial deities as the gods of Canaan were.

views.label: The LORD alone is our God
views.case: The four Hebrew words have no verb, and the BSB footnote lists 'The LORD is our God, the LORD alone' as a possible rendering. On this reading the stress falls on exclusive loyalty, a confession of allegiance fitted to a people surrounded by many gods. Zechariah 14:9, 'the LORD alone, and His name alone,' uses the same word in this sense.

views.label: Oneness that later revelation fills out
views.case: Paul restates the Shema in 1 Corinthians 8:6, 'one God, the Father ... one Lord, Jesus Christ,' placing Jesus within the confession rather than beside it. Some appeal to 'one flesh' in Genesis 2:24 to show that echad can describe a unity of more than one, though the word itself simply means 'one.' The stronger ground is the New Testament's own use of the text, not the lexicon.

debates.bearing: The first two readings are close, and both are true to Deuteronomy: the LORD is the only God, and therefore Israel must have no other. The Christian confession of the Trinity is not what Moses meant his hearers to grasp, but it is a confession of one God, and the New Testament presents it as faithful to the Shema, not a departure from it.

debates.question: What does verse 25 mean by 'that will be our righteousness'?

views.label: Obedience as the way to earn standing with God
views.case: Some read the verse as describing a righteousness by law-keeping, which Paul contrasts with faith in Romans 10:5, citing Leviticus 18:5, 'The man who does these things will live by them.' On this view the verse shows what the law demands and why no one achieves it, Galatians 3:10-12.

views.label: Covenant faithfulness of a redeemed people
views.case: Others note that the verse is the end of an answer that began with rescue: 'We were slaves ... but the LORD brought us out,' verse 21. Righteousness here is the fitting response of people already saved. Deuteronomy 24:13 uses the same phrase of an act of kindness that 'will be credited to you as righteousness before the LORD,' the language of Genesis 15:6.

debates.bearing: The context favours the second reading for Moses' own meaning: the order is grace, then command, then a life that is right before God. Paul's contrast in Romans 10 is aimed at a pursuit of righteousness 'as if it were by works,' Romans 9:32, which cuts the command off from the grace that grounds it. Paul himself quotes Deuteronomy 30:14 for the word of faith, Romans 10:8.

debates.question: Were the commands of verses 8 and 9 meant literally?

views.label: Literal practice
views.case: The commands are concrete: tie, bind, write. Jewish tradition took them literally, producing tefillin and the mezuzah, and Jesus never condemns the practice, only its display, Matthew 23:5.

views.label: Figurative language
views.case: Exodus 13:9 and 13:16 use the same language of the Passover festival, which could not literally be tied to a hand, so the words may describe a life marked by the law as vividly as a sign on the body. Proverbs 3:3 and 7:3 use similar images, binding teaching around the neck or tying it to the fingers, alongside writing it 'on the tablet of your heart.'

debates.bearing: The purpose is the same either way: God's words on the heart, verse 6, shaping what the hands do, what the mind attends to, and what happens in the home. A literal practice that leaves the heart untouched misses the point, and a figurative reading that leaves the life untouched misses it just as much.

study.originalLanguages:
The Shema itself is four Hebrew words after 'Hear, O Israel': YHWH eloheinu YHWH echad. Hebrew often omits the verb 'to be,' so the words can be divided in more than one way, as the BSB footnote shows: 'The LORD our God is One LORD,' 'The LORD is our God, the LORD is One,' or 'The LORD is our God, the LORD alone.' The main text chooses a double statement, 'The LORD our God, the LORD is One.' Every option confesses both that the LORD is Israel's God and that He is unrivalled; the options differ on which note sounds loudest.

The three 'all' phrases of verse 5 are worth separating. Levav, heart, is the centre of the person in Hebrew thought, the place of understanding, decision and will as well as feeling; in Deuteronomy 29:4 the BSB renders the same word 'a mind to understand.' Nephesh, soul, is not an immaterial part of a person but the whole living self, the word used when Genesis 2:7 says the man became a living being. Me'od, strength, is striking because elsewhere it is almost always the adverb 'very' or 'exceedingly.' Here it is used as a noun, something like 'muchness,' all that one has and is capable of. The same three words appear together of Josiah in 2 Kings 23:25. When the Gospels quote the verse they use four terms, heart, soul, mind and strength, Mark 12:30, drawing out the understanding that levav already includes.

'Teach them diligently' in verse 7 translates a single verb, shinnantam, from shanan, which normally means to sharpen or whet. God uses it of sharpening His sword in Deuteronomy 32:41. The picture is of repeated, careful teaching that puts an edge on the words in a child's mind, not an occasional lesson.

The 'reminders' on the forehead in verse 8 are totaphot, the word used in the same hand and forehead phrase in Exodus 13:16 and Deuteronomy 11:18. The 'doorposts' of verse 9 are mezuzot, the same word used for the doorframes daubed with the blood of the Passover lamb, Exodus 12:7. The household once marked by blood on the night of rescue is now to be marked by the word of the God who rescued it.

Verse 13 gathers three verbs of allegiance. Yare, fear, means reverence that shapes life; avad, serve, is the word for the service of a slave or a worshipper, and it answers the 'house of slavery' in verse 12, since Israel changes masters; and taking oaths 'in His name' means calling on Him alone as witness. When Jesus quotes the verse in Matthew 4:10 He answers a demand for worship with the command to serve God only.

Finally, 'righteousness' in verse 25 is tsedaqah, the noun of Genesis 15:6, where Abram's faith was 'credited to him as righteousness,' and of Deuteronomy 24:13. In Deuteronomy it describes conduct that is right before the LORD within the covenant He has already made.

typology.type: Israel, God's son, tested at Massah (v.16)
typology.fulfillment: Israel was God's firstborn son, Exodus 4:22, brought through the sea and then tested in the wilderness, where at Massah they demanded proof, 'Is the LORD among us or not?' Exodus 17:7. Jesus, declared the beloved Son at His baptism, is led into the wilderness and tempted to throw Himself from the temple to force God's hand. He answers from verse 16, 'Do not put the Lord your God to the test,' Matthew 4:7, and from verse 13, 'serve Him only,' Matthew 4:10. Where the nation tested God, the Son trusted Him. The correspondence breaks at the decisive point: Israel failed and needed forgiveness; Jesus succeeded and provides it.

typology.type: The one who loves God with all heart, soul and strength (v.5)
typology.fulfillment: The Shema describes a person no Israelite fully was. Even Josiah, who turned to the LORD with heart, soul and strength, 2 Kings 23:25, could not reverse the nation's course. Jesus is the first human being to love God entirely. He says, 'I do exactly what the Father has commanded Me, so that the world may know that I love the Father,' John 14:31, and He goes to the cross in that obedience. The escalation is that His love does not stay His alone. God pours out His love into believers' hearts through the Holy Spirit, Romans 5:5, fulfilling the promise of Deuteronomy 30:6.

typology.type: The words bound on hand and forehead (v.8)
typology.fulfillment: Israel was to wear God's words on the hand and forehead, marking what they did and what they thought as belonging to Him. Revelation takes up the same two places. The beast demands a mark 'on their right hand or on their forehead,' Revelation 13:16, the counterfeit sign of a rival allegiance, while the Lamb's people bear 'His name and His Father's name written on their foreheads,' Revelation 14:1. In the new creation 'His name will be on their foreheads,' Revelation 22:4. The escalation is that God writes His own name on His people; the type falls short because a written sign could be worn without love.

typology.type: The child's question and the story of rescue (vv.20-23)
typology.fulfillment: Israel's answer to a child was a story: 'We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt, but the LORD brought us out,' verse 21. The New Testament gives believers the same shape of confession. Paul writes, 'though you once were slaves to sin ... you have been set free from sin,' Romans 6:17-18. At the Lord's Supper the church does what Israel did at Passover, rehearsing its rescue: 'you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes,' 1 Corinthians 11:26. The escalation is in what is escaped and what is entered: not Pharaoh but sin and death, and not Canaan but a city 'whose architect and builder is God,' Hebrews 11:10.

study.christ:
The clearest link is Jesus' own use of the chapter. Asked which commandment is most important, He quotes the Shema and the command to love, Mark 12:29-30, and then joins it to Leviticus 19:18, 'Love your neighbor as yourself.' He does not choose a command from a list; He identifies the one from which the others hang, Matthew 22:40. The scribe's reply, that loving God and neighbour is 'more important than all burnt offerings and sacrifices,' earns Jesus' verdict, 'You are not far from the kingdom of God,' Mark 12:33-34. He is not far because the One who can bring him in is standing before him.

Jesus also lived the chapter under pressure. Matthew's temptation account follows Israel's wilderness story closely. Jesus is the Son, Matthew 3:17, led into the wilderness for forty days as Israel was led for forty years. Two of His three answers come from Deuteronomy 6. When the devil urges Him to force God to prove His care, He replies from verse 16, 'Do not put the Lord your God to the test,' Matthew 4:7. When the devil offers the kingdoms of the world for a single act of worship, He replies from verse 13, 'Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only,' Matthew 4:10. The Son whose Father had just said 'This is My beloved Son' did not need to test that love.

The New Testament goes further and places Jesus within the Shema. Paul, writing about idols, says, 'there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came ... And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came,' 1 Corinthians 8:6. The words 'God' and 'Lord' of Deuteronomy 6:4 are divided between the Father and the Son without making two gods. Jesus Himself says, 'I and the Father are one,' John 10:30, and that all should honour the Son just as they honour the Father, John 5:23. Philippians 2:10-11 applies to Jesus the confession Isaiah 45:23 reserves for the LORD, that every knee will bow.

This also explains how the command can be kept. No one loves God with all the heart by effort. Jesus loved the Father perfectly, John 14:31, and gave Himself for those who had not. Through Him God pours His love into believers' hearts by the Spirit, Romans 5:5, and so begins to fulfil Deuteronomy 30:6. John's summary is exact: 'We love because He first loved us,' 1 John 4:19. The child's question of verse 20 now receives a fuller answer, the story of a greater exodus accomplished in Christ, and the command to love God becomes the response of those who have been loved.
study.god:
The chapter's central statement about God is His oneness, and it is a statement about both His being and His claim. He is not one god among the many worshipped by the peoples around Israel, verse 14. He is the one God, and because He is one, He can be loved with an undivided heart. A worshipper of many gods divides his loyalty; a worshipper of the LORD owes all of himself to one.

He is the God who acts in history. The chapter's name for Him is repeatedly tied to deeds: He 'brought you out of the land of Egypt,' verse 12; He 'inflicted great and devastating signs and wonders,' verse 22; He 'brought us out from there to lead us in,' verse 23. He is known not by speculation but by what He has done, and the child's question is answered by recounting those deeds.

He is generous. The land He gives is full of what Israel did not make, verses 10 and 11. His commands are given 'that we may always be prosperous and preserved,' verse 24, and Deuteronomy 10:13 says they are 'for your own good.' The God who commands is not taking from His people but giving to them.

He is jealous, verse 15, and He is 'among you.' The two statements belong together. His nearness is what makes idolatry so serious; a husband present in the house cannot be indifferent to unfaithfulness. His anger is real, and the chapter does not soften it. Yet His jealousy protects the relationship. He will not let His people give themselves to gods who cannot save.

He will not be tested, and yet He tests. Israel is forbidden to put Him to the proof as at Massah, verse 16, because that treats His faithfulness as uncertain. Deuteronomy 8:2 will show God testing Israel, a very different thing: the Creator examining the heart for its good. The creature demanding proof of God is presumption; God probing the creature is fatherly care.

Above all, this God asks for love. The command of verse 5 reveals what kind of God He is. He is not satisfied with outward service, sacrifice or fear alone. He wants the heart, the life and all one's strength, the kind of devotion that can only be given freely. That He asks for love means He is personal and relational, and it means He has first loved, Deuteronomy 7:8. The command sets the direction of worship: every act of praise, every obedience, and every lesson to a child is meant to be love returned to the God who is one.

crossReferences.note: Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 6:4-5 as the most important commandment and pairs it with Leviticus 19:18. The scribe's agreement that loving God is more than sacrifices shows that the Shema was already understood as the heart of the law, and Jesus tells him he is not far from the kingdom.

In His wilderness testing Jesus answers the devil from Deuteronomy three times, quoting 6:16 and 6:13 as well as 8:3. He relives Israel's wilderness trial as the obedient Son, refusing to test God and refusing to worship anyone but Him.

The original Massah incident. Israel quarrelled for water and asked, 'Is the LORD among us or not?' Deuteronomy 6:15-16 answers that the LORD is among them and forbids them ever to treat Him that way again. Psalm 95:8-9 keeps the warning alive for later worshippers.

Moses repeats the practices of 6:6-9, binding, teaching and writing the words, and attaches the promise that their days and their children's days will be multiplied in the land. The repetition marks the Shema's practices as central to the whole sermon.

The command of 6:5 returns as a promise: God will circumcise Israel's hearts so that they will love Him with all their heart and soul. What Israel could not produce, God undertakes to give, anticipating the new covenant.

Josiah is described with the Shema's three terms, turning to the LORD with all his heart, soul and strength, after the book of the law was found. He shows what the command looks like in a life, and his reform shows that even the best king could not change the nation's heart.

Paul restates the Shema against idolatry, 'there is no God but one,' and then confesses one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ. The confession of Deuteronomy 6:4 is not abandoned but opened to include the Son.

The prophet looks to the day when the LORD will be King over all the earth, 'the LORD alone, and His name alone.' The confession Israel made in its tents becomes the confession of the whole world at the end.

The psalmist obeys Deuteronomy 6:7 and 6:20-23, declaring God's works to the next generation so that children yet unborn would trust God and not forget His works. It shows the chapter's household teaching extended into Israel's worship.

Joshua reminds Israel that God gave them cities they did not build and vineyards they did not plant, fulfilling Deuteronomy 6:10-11. His challenge, 'choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve,' Joshua 24:15, is the Shema pressed at the moment the danger of the land arrived.

James quotes the confession 'God is one' and warns that even demons believe it and shudder. Deuteronomy 6 never allowed the Shema to be a bare statement; verse 5 follows at once with love, and James presses the same point.

The Lamb's people bear His name and His Father's name on their foreheads. The image takes up the words bound on the forehead in Deuteronomy 6:8 and contrasts them with the beast's mark on hand or forehead, Revelation 13:16.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning the question of Scripture has been whom humanity will trust and love. In Eden the first couple listened to another voice and doubted God's goodness. At Babel humanity united around its own name. The rest of Genesis shows families and nations serving many gods. Deuteronomy 6 is God's answer for His redeemed people: one God, loved with the whole self, His words carried into every home. The confession that the LORD is one is the reversal of every divided loyalty since the fall.

The chapter also shows what will go wrong. Moses foresees Israel eating and being satisfied and forgetting, verses 11 and 12, and the story bears him out. Within a generation after Joshua 'another generation rose up who did not know the LORD,' Judges 2:10; the household teaching of verse 7 had failed. Kings and people turned to other gods until the land was lost. Even Josiah's wholehearted reform, 2 Kings 23:25, could not reverse the tide. The command to love was clear; the heart to obey was missing.

Deuteronomy itself points ahead to the remedy. God promises to circumcise their hearts so that they will love Him, Deuteronomy 30:6, and the prophets promise a new heart and God's Spirit, Ezekiel 36:26-27. In Jesus the command is finally kept. He loves the Father perfectly, John 14:31, resists the testing Israel failed, Matthew 4:7, and gives His Spirit so that God's love is poured into His people's hearts, Romans 5:5. The Shema is now confessed as one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, 1 Corinthians 8:6.

The story ends where the Shema has always pointed. Zechariah 14:9 foresees the LORD as King over all the earth, His name the only name. Philippians 2:10-11 foresees every knee bowing to Jesus to the glory of God the Father. In the new creation God's people will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads, Revelation 22:4, the final form of the words once bound on Israel's foreheads. There the command to love God with all one's heart will no longer be a struggle against a divided self, but the free and unending life of a people made whole.

sermon.title: Knowing God
sermon.why: Keller preaches directly through the Shema and its call to wholehearted love, showing how knowing God rightly, not mere religious duty, is what this chapter and the greatest commandment are actually asking for.

quiz.q: What is the significance of Jesus quoting Deuteronomy 6:4-5 in the Gospels?

options.text: He named it the greatest commandment, foundational for every other command including love of neighbor.
options.note: Mark 12:29-31 records Jesus quoting this passage and naming it first and greatest.

options.text: He rejected it as an outdated rule no longer binding.
options.note: Jesus affirms it as the greatest commandment, the opposite of rejecting it.

options.text: He said it applied only to a future generation of Israel.
options.note: Jesus applies it as a present, universal command, not a future-only one.

options.text: He never referenced this passage.
options.note: Mark 12:29-31 records Jesus quoting it directly.

quiz.q: What does verse 4 mean by declaring 'the LORD is One'?

options.text: It declares the LORD's exclusive, undivided uniqueness; there is no other god to divide Israel's loyalty.
options.note: In its context this functions as a polemical declaration of God's uniqueness against the many gods of the nations.

options.text: It means Israel worships exactly one idol among several available options.
options.note: The verse rules out worship of any other god at all, not a choice among several.

options.text: It means God is an impersonal force rather than a personal being.
options.note: The whole passage addresses God relationally, as one to be loved with heart, soul, and strength, not an impersonal force.

options.text: It has no bearing on how Israel is to worship.
options.note: Verse 5 immediately draws out its direct bearing on how Israel is to love and worship God.

quiz.q: How are parents instructed to teach God's words to their children (vv.6-9)?

options.text: Continually, in ordinary daily moments at home and on the road, and marked visibly as reminders.
options.note: Verses 6-9 describe teaching woven into everyday rhythms of life, not confined to a single formal setting.

options.text: Only once a year at a single festival.
options.note: The text describes constant, daily teaching, not an annual event.

options.text: Only through professional priests.
options.note: The command is addressed directly to parents, not delegated to priests.

options.text: Children are not to be taught these words at all.
options.note: Verses 7 and 20-25 give extensive instruction for teaching children specifically.

quiz.q: What warning does Moses give about the good land Israel is about to receive (vv.10-12)?

options.text: That when they enjoy houses, wells, and vineyards they did not build, they must be careful not to forget the LORD.
options.note: Verses 10-12 give this exact warning about the danger prosperity poses to remembering God.

options.text: That the land would be barren and unproductive.
options.note: The land is described as full of abundance, the opposite of barren.

options.text: That they must never build any houses in the land.
options.note: The warning concerns forgetting God amid abundance, not a prohibition on building.

options.text: No warning at all is given about the land.
options.note: Verses 10-12 give an explicit, pointed warning.

quiz.q: What does Moses forbid in verse 16 regarding testing the LORD?

options.text: Testing Him as Israel did at Massah, presuming on God rather than trusting Him.
options.note: Verse 16 explicitly references the incident at Massah as the pattern to avoid.

options.text: Asking God any questions at all in prayer.
options.note: The command addresses presumptuous testing, not honest questioning or prayer.

options.text: Building altars in His honor.
options.note: Altar-building is not addressed in this verse at all.

options.text: Nothing is forbidden here regarding testing God.
options.note: Verse 16 gives an explicit prohibition.

questions: Jesus calls this the greatest commandment. Is loving God with all your heart, soul, and strength actually the animating center of your life, or has something else quietly taken first place?

Moses commands that God's words be taught continually, woven into ordinary moments of daily life. Where do conversations about God happen naturally in your home and relationships, and where are they conspicuously absent?

Moses warns that prosperity itself, houses you did not build, blessings you did not earn, is one of the greatest threats to remembering God. How is comfort or abundance currently shaping your sense of dependence on Him?
Israel tested God at Massah by demanding proof rather than trusting His track record. Where are you tempted to demand a new sign from God rather than trusting what He has already shown you?
The Shema calls for love that involves heart, soul, and strength, the whole person. Which part of yourself do you find hardest to actually give over to God right now?

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew can be rendered 'the LORD is one' or 'the LORD alone', and both readings agree on the verse's central point, exclusive devotion to the one true God against every rival.
'Love' (ahav) in covenant contexts describes loyal, active devotion expressed in obedience, not primarily an emotional feeling, though it certainly includes the heart.
'As you tested Him at Massah' refers back to the incident in Exodus 17:1-7, when Israel demanded proof of God's presence rather than trusting what He had already shown them.
